title: Introduction
intro: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning at a glance, latent variables and ethical questions.

questions.q: A model estimates the price of a house from its floor area and number of bedrooms. What type of problem is this?
opts: Regression, because the model outputs a continuous number
Binary classification, because the price is either above or below market value
Multiclass classification with one class per price band
Unsupervised learning, because no expert sets the price
questions.exp: Regression returns a continuous value rather than a category assignment. Price bands would be an artificial discretization that the book does not use.

questions.q: A model predicts both the freezing point and the boiling point of a molecule. What is this problem called?
opts: Multivariate regression
Binary classification with the classes solid and liquid
Multiclass classification with two outputs
Conditional generation
questions.exp: The model predicts more than one continuous number. Having several outputs makes the regression multivariate.

questions.q: What does the output vector of a classification model with N categories contain?
opts: The probability that the input belongs to each of the N categories
The index of the chosen category as a single integer
A continuous value that is then rounded to the nearest category
One Boolean value per input feature
questions.exp: The model returns a vector of size N containing class probabilities. The actual class decision is derived from it afterwards.

questions.q: Why are the features of a house considered tabular data?
opts: They have no internal structure. If we reorder the inputs and train a new model, the prediction stays the same.
They are usually stored in a database table.
They consist only of fixed-length integers.
The order of the features carries the meaning of the data.
questions.exp: The defining property is the lack of internal structure. In text, a different word order changes the meaning, and in images, neighboring pixels carry information.

questions.q: Apart from their size, what distinguishes image inputs from tabular data?
opts: Spatial structure: vertically adjacent pixels are closely related even though they are far apart in the input vector
Images always have variable length
Images cannot be represented as a vector of numbers
Image pixels are statistically independent of each other
questions.exp: Concatenating the RGB values destroys vertical neighborhoods. A good model still has to exploit this structure, which later motivates convolutional networks.

questions.q: What does it mean to train a model, in the book's sense?
opts: Searching a family of possible equations for the one that describes the training data best
Storing all training pairs and interpolating between them
Deriving the model equation symbolically from the data
Extending the architecture until every training point is hit exactly
questions.exp: The model defines a family of curves. Training uses the training data to select one member of that family.

questions.q: Where does the term supervised learning come from?
opts: Labeled input/output pairs act as a teacher or supervisor for the training process
A human monitors the predictions during operation
The model supervises its own uncertainty
Experts clean the training data before training
questions.exp: The labels, such as the genre of a music clip identified by an expert, act as the supervisor.

questions.q: Semantic segmentation and machine translation both produce structured outputs. Why is translation considered harder?
opts: The output is ambiguous and must follow its own grammar, which is not closely tied to the input
Text has more dimensions than an image
Translation is a classification problem with millions of classes
Segmentation does not need training data
questions.exp: In segmentation, the output structure is closely tied to the input, and similar neighboring pixels probably share a label. In translation there are several valid outputs, and not every string of words is a valid sentence.

questions.q: According to the book, how can the grammar of a structured output be learned?
opts: Without output labels, from the statistics of large corpora, that is, unsupervised
Only through explicitly programmed grammar rules
By collecting more labeled input/output pairs
Through reinforcement learning with a reward per correct sentence
questions.exp: Valid sentences can be learned from a large text corpus without any pairs. This is the connection to unsupervised learning.

questions.q: What is the goal of the generative unsupervised models the book focuses on?
opts: To synthesize new examples that are statistically indistinguishable from the training data
To partition the training data into clusters
To predict a missing label for every example
To compress the training data losslessly
questions.exp: Some generative models describe the probability distribution explicitly, others only learn a mechanism for generating new examples.

questions.q: Image inpainting and text completion are examples of what?
opts: Conditional generation, where part of the output is predetermined
Multivariate regression
Semantic segmentation
Reinforcement learning
questions.exp: In inpainting, the unobscured pixels stay fixed. In text completion, the beginning of the text is fixed. The model only generates the missing part.

questions.q: A large language model answers a question correctly. What follows from this according to the book?
opts: It generated the most likely completion of the document. It knows the statistics of language but does not understand the significance of its answer.
It built an explicit world model and reasoned logically from it
It retrieved the answer verbatim from its training data
It was trained with supervision on exactly this question
questions.exp: The book stresses that the apparent intelligence comes from filling in the most likely completion.

questions.q: Why can the variation in face images of the same person be described with about 42 numbers?
opts: The images are generated by a physical process with few degrees of freedom, here roughly 42 facial muscles
The image is downscaled to 42 pixels
42 color channels are enough for a face
A classifier distinguishes 42 facial expressions
questions.exp: Real-world images are a tiny subset of all possible RGB combinations. The data is lower dimensional than the number of pixels suggests. This is the core idea behind latent variables.

questions.q: How does a generative model with latent variables create a new example?
opts: It samples from a simple distribution over the latent variables and maps the sample to data space with a deep network
It randomly combines patches of training examples
It finds the most similar training example and adds noise
It draws uniformly distributed random values pixel by pixel
questions.exp: The latent distribution is simple by design. All the complexity lives in the learned mapping from latent space to data space.

questions.q: Why do intermediate images look plausible when interpolating in latent space, rather than like a cross-fade?
opts: The latent variables of the two images are interpolated, and only then mapped back to image space
The pixel values of both images are averaged with weights
The model picks real training images that lie between the two
The images are normalized to the same brightness beforehand
questions.exp: Every sensible point in latent space yields a plausible image. Averaging pixels, in contrast, leaves the set of realistic images.

questions.q: Which statement is NOT an advantage of latent variables when mapping text to images?
opts: The model no longer needs any training data
Fewer text/image pairs are needed because inputs and outputs are lower dimensional
Generated images are more likely to be plausible
Randomness in the mapping produces several images that fit one caption
questions.exp: The book names exactly three advantages: fewer pairs, more plausible images and multiple outputs per caption. Training data is still required.

questions.q: A chess agent receives a reward only at the end of the game, for winning. Which problem becomes extreme here?
opts: Temporal credit assignment: it is unclear which of the many moves were instrumental to success or failure
The exploration-exploitation trade-off
Overfitting to known openings
Missing labels for each board position
questions.exp: The reward arrives long after the actions. Attributing it to the actions that caused it is the temporal credit assignment problem.

questions.q: A robot makes progress by lying on its side and pushing with one leg. Which dilemma does this illustrate?
opts: Exploration vs. exploitation: keep using a known strategy with modest rewards, or try new actions that might lead to walking
Temporal credit assignment
Underfitting of the locomotion model
Non-deterministic state transitions
questions.exp: The known strategy yields reliable but small rewards. Only exploration can discover the much better solution.

questions.q: Why do actions in chess change the state of the system non-deterministically?
opts: For any move, the opponent may respond with many different moves
The rules of chess contain random elements
The agent chooses its moves at random
The reward is transmitted with noise
questions.exp: The agent's own move is unambiguous, but the next state it observes depends on the opponent's response.

questions.q: What does a policy network map?
opts: The observed world state to an action, such as board position to move, or sensor measurements to joint movements
An action to the expected reward
The latent space to the data space
Training data to model parameters
questions.exp: The policy is the mapping from state to action. It is one way to incorporate deep networks into reinforcement learning.

questions.q: A system predicts salary levels from historical data. What does the book say to expect?
opts: It will reproduce historical biases, for example predicting that women should be paid less
It will automatically correct historical biases
It becomes neutral given enough data
It predicts the same mean for all groups
questions.exp: The model learns the relationship the data shows, including its injustices. Careless deployment can entrench or aggravate existing biases.

questions.q: Which approach to explainable AI does the book describe as moderately successful?
opts: Local explanations of why a particular individual decision was made
Full disclosure of how large networks work
Inspection of all weights by experts
Replacing the network with an equivalent rule base
questions.exp: The whole system cannot be explained. For individual decisions, interpretable descriptions are possible. Whether full transparency is achievable remains an open question.

questions.q: A client wants to predict the remaining useful life of a bearing, in operating hours, from vibration data. Which classification fits?
opts: Supervised regression with a time series as input, whose order carries information
Binary classification with tabular data
An unsupervised generative model
Reinforcement learning, because the machine learns during operation
questions.exp: The output is a continuous quantity, labeled through historical failures. Like audio, the input is high dimensional and temporally ordered.

questions.q: An inline inspection system should assign each part image to one of five defect types or to the class OK. What does the model output?
opts: A vector with six probabilities, one per class
A single number between zero and five
A binary mask of the defect regions
A text describing the defect
questions.exp: Six classes make this a multiclass classification problem with N equal to six. A binary mask would instead be a segmentation, which is a structured output.
